core: Working definition of depreciation: spreading the cost of a long-lived asset over its useful life rather than expensing it in the purchase year
Why it exists: the matching idea, an asset serves many periods so its cost is spread to the periods that benefit
Straight-line method as the method to teach: (cost − salvage value) ÷ useful life, equal amount each year, with an original delivery-van worked example
Book value (cost less accumulated depreciation) and accumulated depreciation as the running total
Other methods named in one line each: declining balance and units of production
Depreciation vs market value: book spreading is not a valuation of what the asset could sell for
Book depreciation vs tax depreciation: one factual line that they differ (MACRS in the U.S.), no tax advice
Honest framing: depreciation is a spreading rule, not a valuation; land is not depreciated
supporting: Useful life and salvage (residual) value as the two estimates that feed the formula
Depreciable base as cost minus salvage value
Depreciation expense on the income statement; book value and accumulated depreciation on the balance sheet
Matching as part of accrual accounting (accrual accounting is a sibling topic, referenced only)
outOfScope: Adjusting entries and the mechanics of recording depreciation (sibling topic adjusting-entries)
Tax rules, MACRS recovery periods, or any tax advice
IFRS revaluation of long-lived assets (noted in sources, not taught)

claims.claim: Depreciation is the process of spreading (allocating) the cost of a long-lived asset over its useful life, rather than charging the full cost as an expense of the purchase period.

The reason for depreciation is matching: an asset that serves the business over several periods has its cost matched to those periods and to the revenue it helps generate, so no single year is distorted by a big purchase.
The straight-line method charges an equal amount of depreciation each year, computed as (cost − salvage value) ÷ useful life; it is the most widely used and easiest method.

Useful life is the length of time an asset will be productively used within operations, and salvage (residual) value is the estimated price the asset will sell for or be worth as a trade-in when its useful life ends; both are estimates made when the asset is placed in service.

Book value is an asset's original cost less accumulated depreciation, and accumulated depreciation is the running total of depreciation charged on the asset since purchase; the asset account stays at historical cost and is offset by accumulated depreciation.

The calculation of depreciation expense is not based on anticipated changes in the asset's fair market value; it is an allocation of the asset's cost over its useful life, so book value and market value can differ.

Beyond straight-line, the common depreciation methods include declining balance, which charges more in early years (accelerated), and units of production, which ties expense to actual usage; all spread the same total cost on different schedules.
Land is not depreciated because it is assumed to have an unlimited useful life, and a fully depreciated asset remains on the books at its salvage value until sold or scrapped.

The depreciation a company reports in its financial statements (book depreciation) is computed under accounting rules, while tax depreciation follows tax rules; in the United States the tax depreciation system is MACRS (Modified Accelerated Cost Recovery System).

conflictingEvidence.issue: Whether straight-line is 'the' depreciation method or one of several common methods.
positions: CFI calls straight-line the most widely used and easiest method to calculate.
OpenStax presents straight-line, units-of-production, and double-declining-balance as the three most popular options a company can choose.
conflictingEvidence.resolution: The lesson teaches straight-line in full as the core method at this literacy level and names declining balance and units of production in one line each, without comparing them in depth.

conflictingEvidence.issue: Whether depreciation tracks an asset's loss of value or is purely a cost-allocation rule.
positions: OpenStax states the depreciation calculation is not based on anticipated changes in the asset's fair market value.
A common informal view treats depreciation as measuring how much an asset has declined in resale value.
conflictingEvidence.resolution: The lesson teaches depreciation strictly as cost allocation, explicitly contrasts book value with market value, and flags the market-value misconception in Common Mistakes.

unsupportedExistingClaims: The phase-2 machine-generated draft contained no substantive accounting claims about depreciation (it defined the topic only as 'a foundational Accounting concept' and compared it to a toolbox label); nothing from it was carried into the lesson.
correctionsNeeded: Replaced the generic machine-generated draft with a sourced lesson that defines depreciation as cost allocation over useful life, teaches the straight-line formula with an original worked example, and adds the matching rationale, book-value mechanics, market-value distinction, and a single factual line on book vs tax depreciation.
